title: How to Create a Debt-Repayment Plan Using the Snowball Method
description: Why paying off the smallest balance first works better for human psychology.
content:
Mathematically, the best way to pay off debt is the 'Avalanche Method' (highest interest rate first). However, personal finance is 20% head knowledge and 80% behavior. The **Debt Snowball**, popularized by Dave Ramsey, focuses on behavior modification. By paying off your debts from smallest balance to largest balance—ignoring interest rates—you get quick wins. Seeing a debt hit $0 gives you the dopamine hit and momentum required to stick to the plan for the long haul.

Key Takeaways

  • Momentum > Math: If you have a $500 debt and a $10,000 debt, paying off the $500 one in a month makes you feel like a winner. Tackling the $10,000 one takes years and feels like a grind.
  • Freed Cash Flow: When you kill a small debt, you eliminate its minimum payment. You roll that cash into the next debt payment, creating a growing 'Snowball' of cash flow.
  • Behavioral Change: The Snowball forces you to list all debts and confront reality. The organization alone often reduces anxiety.
  • Exceptions: If you have a Payday Loan (300% interest), kill that first regardless of balance. That is a financial fire.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US consumer debt is often fragmented across 5-10 accounts (3 credit cards, 2 car loans, 4 student loans). The Snowball method is particularly effective in the US system because it reduces the number of bills you track, simplifying your financial life.

The Snowball Simulation

Imagine you have $500 extra per month to throw at debt.

Your Debts

  • Card A: $500 Balance (15% Rate). Min Payment: $25.
  • Card B: $2,000 Balance (24% Rate). Min Payment: $60.
  • Car Loan: $10,000 Balance (6% Rate). Min Payment: $300.

Month 1

Pay minimums on Card B and Car.
Throw the $500 surplus + $25 minimum at Card A.
Result: Card A is paid off in 1 month. Boom. Win.

Month 2

You now have the $500 surplus + the $25 you used to pay on Card A.
New 'Snowball' = $525/month.
Attack Card B.
Result: Card B is gone in ~4 months.

Month 6

You now have $500 + $25 + $60 = $585/month extra to attack the Car.
You are debt-free years faster because you didn't quit.

Setting It Up

  1. List Everything: Write down every debt, balance, and minimum payment. Sort by Balance (Low to High). Ignore the interest rate column.
  2. Automate Minimums: Set auto-pay for the minimums on everything so you never pay a late fee.
  3. Manual Attack: Manually push the extra money to the #1 debt on payday. Do not wait until the end of the month.
  4. Cut the Plastic: You cannot get out of a hole while digging. Stop using the cards while you pay them off.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this cost me more interest?

Yes. Mathematically, you pay more interest than the Avalanche method. But if you quit the Avalanche method because you get discouraged, you pay the most interest. The best plan is the one you stick to.

Should I close the cards?

Wait. Closing cards can hurt your credit score (Credit Utilization Ratio). Keep them open with a $0 balance unless you are tempted to use them.

What about my mortgage?

Do not include the mortgage in the Snowball. That is a long-term asset. Focus on consumer debt first.
